{"id": "f026cd71-fb7f-482a-b252-f5abbd827e25", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "An Application Load Balancer (ALB) works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). A Network Load Balancer (NLB) works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS). Most of the other differences follow from that.

| | **ALB** | **NLB** |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | 7 (application) | 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TCP_UDP, TLS |
| **Routing** | Content-based. Rules match on path, host header, HTTP headers, query strings, methods and source IP. | Connection-based. It routes by IP and port and doesn't inspect the payload. |
| **Performance** | Good for web traffic. It adds more per-request latency because it parses requests. | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency. It handles millions of requests per second and sudden traffic spikes. |
| **Static IPs** | No. You use DNS names, or put Global Accelerator in front. | Yes. It has one static IP per AZ and supports Elastic IPs. |
| **Client source IP** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header. | Preserved by default for instance targets. Proxy Protocol v2 is also available. |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and supports SNI and multiple certificates. | Can terminate TLS or pass it through to targets. |
| **Security groups** | Supported. | Supported (added in 2023), but you must choose this when you create the NLB. |
| **Built-in features** | Authentication through Cognito or OIDC, redirects, fixed responses, and AWS WAF integration. | PrivateLink endpoint services and TLS passthrough. |
| **Target types** | Instances, IPs, Lambda. | Instances, IPs, and ALB (an NLB can front an ALB). |

**When to use an ALB**
- HTTP/HTTPS web apps, APIs, and microservices that need path- or host-based routing, such as `/api` to one service and `/app` to another.
- Container workloads on ECS or EKS that share one load balancer across many services.
- Setups that need WAF, authentication offload, or HTTP-level redirects.

**When to use an NLB**
- Non-HTTP protocols, such as gaming, IoT, streaming, or custom TCP/UDP.
- Workloads that need extreme performance and low latency.
- Setups that need static or Elastic IPs, for example when partners allowlist your IPs.
- Exposing a service privately through AWS PrivateLink.
- End-to-end TLS passthrough, such as mutual TLS handled by the backend.

A common pattern is an NLB in front of an ALB. It gives you static IPs and PrivateLink while keeping Layer 7 routing.

I can also look at the load balancers in your account and suggest which type suits a given workload.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
